lines.text:
Building Intelligence — Inside the Robotics Lab

A robotics lab is where engineering meets imagination. On the workbenches, students assemble machines from components — motors, sensors, gears, wheels, axles, and frames — connecting them with wires and programming them to move, sense, and respond. The goal is not just to build a robot but to understand the principles that make it work.

The electronics are fundamental. A circuit board provides the platform where components are connected. A battery pack supplies power. A resistor controls the flow of electricity. A capacitor stores and releases charge. A transistor acts as a switch or amplifier. A diode allows current to flow in only one direction. A microchip — the brain of the robot — processes instructions from the code. An LED provides visual feedback — a blinking light that confirms the circuit is working. A breadboard allows students to prototype circuits without soldering, pushing components into rows of connected holes.

The mechanical parts give the robot its body. A motor converts electrical energy into movement. Gears change the speed and direction of rotation. Wheels and axles provide mobility. A frame holds everything together. A robotic arm extends the robot's reach. A gripper at the end of the arm picks up objects. A camera module gives the robot vision. Sensors detect the environment — light, distance, temperature, touch.

Tools fill the drawers. A soldering iron melts solder to join wires and components permanently. A multimeter measures voltage, current, and resistance. A screwdriver set handles every size of screw. Pliers grip. A wire cutter trims excess wire. A wire stripper removes insulation. A hot glue gun secures components in place. An Allen key tightens hex bolts. A wrench adjusts nuts. Tweezers handle tiny parts. A magnifying glass and helping hands — a stand with adjustable clips — make detailed work easier.

Programming brings the robot to life. Students sit at a computer with a monitor, keyboard, and mouse, writing instructions in a code editor. The code is uploaded to the microchip via a USB cable. A controller or joystick allows manual operation. A remote control sends wireless commands. A tablet may serve as both a programming interface and a control panel.

The lab produces different types of robots. A humanoid robot walks on two legs and mimics human movement. A drone flies. A robotic arm performs precise tasks in manufacturing. A wheeled robot navigates flat surfaces. A walking robot crosses uneven terrain. A line follower uses sensors to track a black line on a white surface — a classic first project. A sumo robot pushes opponents out of a ring.

Robotics teaches problem-solving. When a motor spins the wrong way, you reverse the wires. When a sensor gives false readings, you recalibrate. When the code crashes, you debug. Every failure teaches something — and in a robotics lab, failure is not a setback but a step forward.

lines.text: 'Robot' comes from the Czech word 'robota' meaning 'forced labour'. It was coined by Karel Capek in his 1920 play 'R.U.R.' (Rossum's Universal Robots). 'Android' = a human-shaped robot. 'Cyborg' = a being that is part human, part machine.

lines.text: British English: 'programme' (general use, TV programme), but 'program' for computer programs. American English: 'program' for everything. 'Programming' and 'programmer' are spelled the same in both varieties.

lines.text: 'Programmed to + infinitive': the purpose structure after passive verbs uses 'to', not 'for + -ing.' 'Designed to detect', 'built to carry', 'programmed to follow.' 'For + -ing' describes general function: 'A sensor for detecting light.' But with a specific subject: 'The sensor was designed to detect light.'

lines.text: In first conditional and zero conditional sentences, use present simple after 'if' — not 'will.' 'If the motor spins..., reverse...' (zero conditional — general truth). 'If the motor spins..., you should reverse...' (first conditional — likely situation). 'Will' goes in the main clause, never the if-clause.

lines.text: Reported/indirect speech requires tense backshift when the reporting verb is past: 'detected that there was' (not 'is'). Present → past: 'The sensor shows there is...' → 'The sensor showed there was...' This backshift rule applies consistently in formal and academic writing at B2 level.
